text.paragraph: Periodic adult preventive visit during treatment for acute myeloid leukemia. [S]

Mrs. Joliot-Curie is a 58-year-old physicist with acute myeloid leukemia, on day 29 of her first cycle of azacitidine with venetoclax, who comes for her yearly preventive visit, which she asked to keep. The nausea and constipation settled within a few days. She has had no fever. The day-22 marrow showed no leukemia under the microscope, and venetoclax is on hold while her counts recover. She is tired but walks a little every day and reads papers from her laboratory at home. She has met the palliative care team twice and the transplant center once. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1955-10-26; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Tired but well; weight 53.2 kg, BMI 20.0; blood pressure 116/70
Fading bruises on the shins; no petechiae; no suspicious moles
No ulcers or thrush; teeth in good repair
Regular rhythm; no murmur; no ankle edema
Fine crackles at the right apex, unchanged; otherwise clear
Soft and non-tender; no enlarged liver or spleen
Two months of tiredness, easy bruising and bleeding gums, with pancytopenia and 12 percent blasts on the blood smear; acute leukemia suspected and urgent hematology review booked
S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the bone marrow diagnosis two days later; its timing echoes the documented decline in her health (D).

Acute myeloid leukemia diagnosed on bone marrow biopsy (34 percent myeloblasts), in a physicist with decades of occupational exposure to ionizing radiation; synthetic modern diagnosis linked to her documented leukemia
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis and subtype; the type of her real leukemia is not documented.

Occupational exposure to ionizing radiation over about four decades: X-ray work early in her career, laboratory work with polonium and other radioactive sources, and a laboratory accident in which a sealed polonium source ruptured on her bench about ten years ago

Pulmonary tuberculosis in her forties, treated to completion; no symptoms of active disease

Follow-up: Response review and cycle 2 decision in four days. COVID-19 vaccine at the next infusion visit. Deferred screening and vaccines to be revisited after treatment or before transplant. Next preventive visit in one year. Next scheduled visit 1955-10-30: count recovery and response assessment; cycle 2; transplant evaluation; occupational dose records. [S]

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 30 minutes, with her consent, building on her first meeting with the palliative care team. She understands that her leukemia is high risk and that a transplant offers the best chance of long remission but carries its own risks. She wants full treatment, including intensive care, while there is a reasonable chance of returning to a life she values, which for her means being able to think, read and talk about her work; she would not want prolonged life support if that were no longer possible. She named a health care agent, recorded in the confidential part of the chart and not named here, and completed an advance directive. To be revisited at each change in her illness. [S]
